introduction-breaking-the-safety-glass.core: Go is safe and simple by design, but it offers escape hatches (reflection, unsafe and cgo) for the rare cases that need runtime type inspection, raw memory or C libraries. Each one trades away safety or simplicity.

first_principles.problem: Engineers reach for escape hatches too early and lose the guarantees that made Go attractive.
truths: Safety rules prevent whole classes of bugs.
Some problems genuinely need lower-level access.
Every escape hatch has a cost.
derivation: **reflection**: work with types unknown at compile time.
Use them **only when there's no safe alternative**, and isolate them.

analogy.title: Breaking the glass on a fire alarm
analogy.story: It's there for emergencies; pulling it routinely causes chaos.
analogy.breaks: Libraries you depend on may use them internally. That's acceptable when it's well tested.

steps.label: Principle
steps.detail: Use one only when the safe path truly can't do the job.

check.q: Name Go's three main escape hatches.

reflection-inspecting-the-unknown.core: The reflect package inspects and manipulates values whose types are only known at runtime (reflect.TypeOf and ValueOf). It powers encoding/json, ORMs and struct-tag-driven configuration.

first_principles.problem: A config loader must fill any struct from environment variables based on its field tags, without knowing the struct type in advance.
truths: Interfaces carry type information at runtime.
Generic tools must handle arbitrary structs.
Struct tags are metadata readable at runtime.

analogy.title: An X-ray of a sealed box
analogy.story: You can't open the box at compile time, but at runtime you can see what's inside and act on it.
analogy.breaks: You lose compile-time checks, so mistakes become runtime panics.

example.title: An env-tag config loader

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Any struct can be configured from its tags.

example.outcome: generic tools work on arbitrary types.

check.q: Why must you use ValueOf(&x).Elem() to set fields?
check.a: Only an addressable value (through a pointer) is settable.

the-cost-of-reflection.core: Reflection is slow (it allocates and does dynamic lookups), unsafe at compile time (panics at runtime) and hard to read. Prefer generics, interfaces or code generation, and confine reflection to boundaries.

first_principles.problem: A hot path using reflection allocates heavily, and a typo in a field name panics in production.
truths: Static code lets the compiler optimise.
Runtime type checks cost CPU and allocations.
Readability is maintainability.
derivation: **Benchmark** before using reflection on hot paths.
Use **codegen** (easyjson, sqlc) for speed with safety.

analogy.title: Asking for directions at every turn
analogy.story: Flexible, but much slower than knowing the route in advance.
analogy.breaks: At configuration or startup time, reflection's cost usually doesn't matter.

example.title: JSON in a high-throughput API

steps.label: Decision
steps.detail: Use codegen on the hot path and reflection elsewhere.

example.outcome: reflection is used only where it's cheap enough.

check.q: What Go feature often replaces reflection for type-agnostic code?

unsafe-pointers-here-be-dragons.core: unsafe.Pointer bypasses Go's type system to reinterpret memory, for example for zero-copy conversions or syscall structures. Misuse corrupts memory, and it can break across Go versions.

first_principles.problem: Converting a large []byte to string copies it, which is expensive in a tight parsing loop.
truths: Type safety forbids reinterpreting bits.
Copies cost time and memory.
The GC and the compiler assume type rules hold.
derivation: Use **unsafe.Pointer** as a bridge between pointer types.
Never **mutate** memory shared through such a conversion.

analogy.title: Removing the guard from a power tool
analogy.story: You can make cuts the guard prevents, but one slip costs a finger.
analogy.breaks: It's not portable between architectures or guaranteed across Go releases.

example.title: Zero-copy byte → string

steps.label: Caveat
steps.detail: If b changes, the 'immutable' string changes too, which is undefined behaviour.

code.text:
s := unsafe.String(unsafe.SliceData(b), len(b))
// b must not be modified afterwards!

example.outcome: you get performance at an explicit risk.

check.q: What's the danger after a zero-copy []byte→string conversion?
check.a: Mutating the byte slice silently changes the supposedly immutable string.

cgo-the-bridge-to-c.core: cgo lets Go call C functions through `import "C"` and a preamble. It's essential when the only implementation is a C library (SQLite, ImageMagick, CUDA).

first_principles.problem: A required capability exists only in a C library, with no pure-Go alternative.
truths: Decades of C libraries exist.
Go and C have different memory models.
Crossing the boundary has a cost.
derivation: Write a **C preamble** in a comment above `import "C"`.

analogy.title: An interpreter at a border crossing
analogy.story: Goods can cross, but each crossing needs paperwork, and the rules differ on each side.
analogy.breaks: Each call costs tens of nanoseconds, so chatty calls across the boundary are slow.

example.title: Calling a C function

steps.label: Note
steps.detail: Every C allocation needs an explicit free.

example.outcome: access to the C ecosystem from Go.

check.q: Why must you call C.free on C.CString results?
check.a: The memory is allocated by C, outside the Go GC, so it would leak.

the-hidden-costs-of-cgo.core: cgo breaks Go's superpowers: no easy cross-compilation, no fully static binaries by default, slower builds, per-call overhead, and crashes in C that take down the whole process.

first_principles.problem: A team adds one cgo dependency and suddenly CI can't cross-compile, images need libc, and a segfault kills the service.
truths: Cross-compiling C needs a C toolchain for each target.
C code is outside Go's safety.
Boundary calls aren't free.
derivation: Watch out for **slow builds** and per-call overhead.
Prefer **pure-Go alternatives** (modernc sqlite) where they exist.

analogy.title: Adding a petrol engine to an electric car
analogy.story: It extends the range, but now you need fuel, oil changes and exhaust, and the car is no longer simple.
analogy.breaks: Sometimes the C library is unavoidable. Then contain it in one package.

example.title: Choosing an SQLite driver
flow: Choose pure Go for CLI tools
example.outcome: cgo is used only when the trade-offs are worth it.

check.a: You need a C compiler and libraries for every target platform.

go-workspaces-the-monorepo-fix.core: A go.work file lists several local modules so they build against each other's working copies. That replaces fragile `replace` directives when you develop across modules in a monorepo.

first_principles.problem: Changing a shared auth module and the service that uses it means temporary `replace` lines that get committed by accident.
truths: Each module resolves its dependencies independently.
Local development needs local versions.
Committed replace directives break other builds.
derivation: **go.work** stays local, so usually don't commit it.

analogy.title: A shared workbench
analogy.story: Instead of mailing parts between workshops, you put all the projects on one bench while you're building.
analogy.breaks: CI should usually build without go.work, so released versions are what actually get tested.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No replace directives, and changes are visible instantly.

code.text:
go work init ./pkg/auth ./services/api
go build ./services/api   # uses local ./pkg/auth

check.q: What do Go workspaces replace in multi-module development?
